cases.case_name: Padgett v. Department of Health & Rehabilitative Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of Florida
cases.holding: Parental rights may be involuntarily terminated only on clear and convincing proof that reunification poses a substantial risk of significant harm to the child and that termination is the least restrictive means of protecting the child, which ordinarily requires a good-faith agency effort to rehabilitate the parent and reunite the family; abuse of one child may supply grounds as to another child.
cases.quote: the state must show by clear and convincing evidence that reunification with the parent poses a substantial risk of significant harm to the child

relevance.DEC-03: Padgett fixes the evidentiary weight a Florida agency finding must ultimately carry if it is to support severance, disciplining what a substantiation can be used for downstream.
relevance.DEC-06: Because the State must ordinarily show a good-faith rehabilitative effort before severance, front-end voluntary or alternative-response service offers are constitutionally significant, not optional niceties.
relevance.ACT-01: Padgett treats a performance agreement or comparable voluntary plan as the ordinary proof that the agency tried rehabilitation before seeking severance.
relevance.ACT-02: The least-restrictive-means requirement obliges the agency to offer a court-approved plan and a genuine chance to comply before pursuing termination.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification is the constitutional default: the State must show reunification itself would risk significant harm before permanency shifts away from the parent.
relevance.OUT-02: This is Florida's controlling standard for involuntary termination of parental rights and the source of the least-restrictive-means test.

cases.case_name: Department of Health & Rehabilitative Services v. M.B.
cases.court: Supreme Court of Florida
cases.holding: A child's out-of-court statements that satisfy section 90.803(23)'s reliability safeguards are admissible as substantive evidence in a dependency hearing even when they are inconsistent with the child's in-court testimony, and dependency itself is proved by a preponderance of the evidence.
cases.quote: are admissible as substantive evidence in a dependency hearing once they have satisfied the stringent reliability safeguards established in section 90.803(23) and refined in our prior case law

relevance.INP-08: School, medical and other third-party disclosures typically reach court as child hearsay, and M.B. sets the reliability gate those statements must clear.
relevance.DEC-03: M.B. supplies the evidentiary basis on which a finding of abuse can rest and the reliability findings a court must make before crediting a child's report.
relevance.DEC-05: When the agency files a dependency petition, M.B. governs what proof it may use and confirms the preponderance standard at adjudication.
relevance.ACT-06: The reliability hearing M.B. requires is the mechanism by which disclosures made during medical or psychological examinations enter the dependency record.

cases.case_name: R.F. v. Florida Department of Children & Families
cases.court: Supreme Court of Florida
cases.holding: Proof that a parent sexually abused one child does not by itself establish that a sibling is dependent; the court must examine all the circumstances to decide whether the parent poses a substantial risk of imminent abuse or neglect to the other child.
cases.quote: While the commission of such an act may be highly relevant, it is not automatically dispositive of the issue of dependency.

relevance.INP-10: When a screened report about one child is escalated to an investigation covering siblings, R.F. bars treating the first child's abuse as automatic proof as to the others.
relevance.DEC-03: A substantiated finding as to one child cannot be mechanically extended to siblings; prospective abuse must be proved on the whole record.
relevance.DEC-05: R.F. governs the sufficiency of a dependency petition that alleges prospective abuse or neglect of a sibling.
relevance.ACT-03: Removal and foster placement of an unharmed sibling requires case-specific proof of substantial risk, not a per se rule.
relevance.OUT-05: Where the circumstances do not show substantial risk to the sibling, the petition as to that child must fail.

cases.case_name: Department of Health & Rehabilitative Services v. Yamuni
cases.court: Supreme Court of Florida
cases.holding: Florida's child welfare agency owes a statutory duty of care to prevent further harm to a child once reports of abuse are received, and caseworker investigation and protective-supervision activity is operational-level conduct for which sovereign immunity is waived under section 768.28.
cases.quote: We agree with the district court below that HRS has a statutory duty of care to prevent further harm to children when reports of child abuse are received.

relevance.INP-01: Yamuni converts the mandatory-report statute into an enforceable duty: once a report arrives, the agency owes the child a duty of care.
relevance.INP-02: The duty attaches to reports from relatives and other non-mandated reporters as well, because the statute directs all persons to report.
relevance.INP-03: Police reports of suspected abuse trigger the same protective duty the agency must then carry out.
relevance.INP-06: Hotline intake is the point at which the statutory duty to prevent further harm begins to run.
relevance.DEC-01: Closing or screening out a case without assigning protective supervision exposed the agency to liability in Yamuni, so screen-out decisions are not immune judgment calls.
relevance.OUT-06: A child's severe injury after repeated reports supported a negligence verdict against the agency.
relevance.FAIL-04: Yamuni is the Florida authority for agency tort liability when a child is harmed after the agency failed to carry out protective supervision.
relevance.PMC-04: Fatality and near-fatality reviews in Florida operate against Yamuni's rule that operational failures after a report are actionable.

cases.case_name: J.B. v. Florida Department of Children & Families
cases.court: Supreme Court of Florida
cases.holding: An indigent parent's right to counsel in termination proceedings includes the right to effective assistance and a procedural means of raising such claims, although J.B. herself showed no basis to set aside the termination order.
cases.quote: we hold that the right to counsel in termination of parental right (TPR) proceedings includes the right to effective assistance and requires a means of vindicating that right

relevance.OUT-02: This decision creates the ineffective-assistance remedy that now accompanies every Florida termination judgment against an indigent parent.

cases.case_name: S.M. v. Florida Department of Children & Families
cases.court: Supreme Court of Florida
cases.holding: Once grounds for termination are proved by clear and convincing evidence and reunification is not in the child's manifest best interests, the least-restrictive-means requirement does not oblige the trial court to consider permanent guardianship instead of adoption.
cases.quote: Section 39.621, Florida Statutes (2016), specifies that permanent guardianship shall be considered only after reunification and adoption are not available options.

relevance.ACT-03: S.M. sets the statutory order of permanency goals that governs planning for a child already in out-of-home care.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification stands first in the statutory hierarchy of permanency goals and must be ruled out before other outcomes.
relevance.OUT-02: S.M. confirms that adoption outranks guardianship once termination grounds are established, limiting the least-restrictive-means argument.
relevance.OUT-03: Permanent guardianship is a subordinate permanency option available only after reunification and adoption are unavailable.

cases.case_name: Statewide Guardian ad Litem Office v. C.C.
cases.court: Supreme Court of Florida
cases.holding: An appellate court may not reweigh the evidence supporting a termination judgment; because competent substantial evidence supported the trial court's least-restrictive-means and manifest-best-interests findings after the father failed a voluntary case plan, the district court's reversal was quashed.
cases.quote: We conclude that the Fifth District's decision improperly reweighed the evidence below and, thus, conflicts with our precedent.

relevance.DEC-06: The Department's initial route was a voluntary, non-adjudicatory case plan, and C.C. shows how that front-end choice is later weighed.
relevance.ACT-01: C.C. treats an accepted and funded voluntary case plan as a genuine rehabilitative effort by the Department.
relevance.ACT-02: The opinion measures reasonable efforts by the services actually offered and paid for under the plan.
relevance.OUT-01: Continued non-compliance after services were provided defeated the reunification goal.
relevance.OUT-02: C.C. is the most recent Florida Supreme Court statement on proof of least restrictive means and manifest best interests in termination cases.
relevance.FAIL-01: It limits when a district court may reverse a dependency or termination judgment: not by reweighing evidence.

cases.case_name: In re D.B.
cases.court: Supreme Court of Florida
cases.holding: Indigent parents have a constitutional right to appointed counsel whenever the proceeding can result in permanent loss of parental custody; in other dependency proceedings the right is determined case by case.
cases.quote: We find that a constitutional right to counsel necessarily arises where the proceedings can result in permanent loss of parental custody.

relevance.DEC-05: When the agency files a petition that can end in permanent loss of custody, D.B. requires the court to appoint counsel for indigent parents.
relevance.OUT-02: D.B. is Florida's foundational right-to-counsel holding for proceedings ending in permanent severance.

cases.case_name: Seminole Tribe of Florida v. Department of Children & Families
cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, Fourth District
cases.holding: A trial court's finding of good cause to deviate from ICWA's placement preferences is reviewed for abuse of discretion, and the deviation was affirmed where the record showed the court understood the statutory scheme and found the tribal family could not presently meet the child's needs.
cases.quote: choosing to apply Florida's abuse of discretion standard to the review of a trial court's finding of good cause to deviate

relevance.INP-11: This is the leading Florida decision applying ICWA's placement-preference scheme once a tribe intervenes in a state dependency case.
relevance.ACT-04: It governs when a court may place an Indian child outside the statutory preference for extended family and tribal homes.
relevance.FAIL-05: Deviation from ICWA preferences requires a reasoned good-cause finding, which is the safeguard against placement decisions that override tribal affiliation.

cases.case_name: J.P.H. v. Florida Department of Children & Families
cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, First District
cases.holding: Termination of parental rights to Indian children was reversed because the trial court applied Florida's clear-and-convincing standard instead of ICWA's beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard and wrongly denied the tribe intervention for lack of Florida counsel.
cases.quote: which requires that any order terminating parental rights to an Indian child be supported "by evidence beyond a reasonable doubt," rather than the clear and convincing evidence standard

relevance.INP-11: J.P.H. is the clearest Florida holding that ICWA displaces Chapter 39's proof standard and guarantees the tribe's right to intervene.

cases.case_name: In re Records of the Department of Children & Family Services (Sarasota Herald-Tribune v. Department of Children & Family Services)
cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, Second District
cases.holding: A circuit court considering a petition for access to confidential child abuse records must conduct an in camera review before ruling; refusing to inspect the records was an abuse of discretion and the denial of access was reversed.
cases.quote: the circuit court abused its discretion when it failed to conduct an in camera review of the records to which the Herald-Tribune seeks access

relevance.INP-06: Hotline reports and investigative records are confidential under section 39.202, and this case sets the procedure for piercing that confidentiality.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the Florida procedure by which the public obtains records after a child dies or is seriously injured in the system.
relevance.FAIL-06: A blanket refusal to review withheld records is itself reversible error, which is the remedy for disclosure failures.
relevance.PMC-03: Independent review of agency performance depends on this in camera mechanism for reaching otherwise confidential files.
relevance.PMC-04: Fatality review work turns on the good-cause balancing and in camera inspection this case requires.
relevance.PMC-05: This is the operative Florida authority for public-records access to child welfare files.
relevance.PMC-06: Any external analysis of Florida case files must proceed through the judicial good-cause process described here.

cases.case_name: Department of Health & Rehabilitative Services v. Gainesville Sun Publishing Co.
cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, First District
cases.holding: A trial court may order confidential child abuse records produced for in camera inspection and may find good cause for disclosure without an evidentiary hearing, balancing the child's and siblings' privacy against the public interest in evaluating agency performance.
cases.quote: Under the circumstances of this case, the trial court did not err in finding good cause for disclosure without an evidentiary hearing.

relevance.INP-09: Public scrutiny of how the agency handled a case is an express component of the good-cause balance, which is how outside oversight is triggered.
relevance.FAIL-06: The decision forecloses the agency's argument that it may withhold records until the requester first proves good cause.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the earliest Florida appellate authority letting the press obtain confidential abuse records on a good-cause showing.

cases.case_name: Urquhart v. Helmich
cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, First District
cases.holding: A physician who reported suspected child abuse was immune from civil liability under section 39.203 because the record showed no evidence overcoming the good-faith presumption, and summary judgment for the reporter was affirmed.
cases.quote: Section 39.203, Florida Statutes affords a general grant of immunity to a person who makes a report of child abuse in good faith.

relevance.INP-01: Urquhart is the Florida appellate application of the reporter-immunity statute that accompanies the universal duty to report.
relevance.INP-02: The same immunity protects any person who reports in good faith, not only professionals.
relevance.INP-06: Good-faith immunity is what makes hotline reporting workable, and this case shows how hard it is to overcome.
relevance.INP-07: The reporter here was a treating physician acting on an emergency-room presentation, the paradigm medical disclosure.
relevance.INP-08: The good-faith standard applied here is the same one that protects teachers and school staff who report.

cases.case_name: Department of Children & Families v. J.D.
cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, Fifth District
cases.holding: The circuit court has jurisdiction to entertain a Department petition for an injunction to protect a child from an alleged abuser even when no dependency case is open, and dismissal for want of jurisdiction was reversed.
cases.quote: The trial court clearly has jurisdiction to entertain petitions for protective injunctions to prevent this type of abuse.

relevance.INP-03: The petition arose from a law-enforcement-referred sexual abuse allegation against a non-caregiver, the classic cross-referral posture.
relevance.INP-04: It confirms the court's own authority to act on a protection petition outside an existing dependency case.
relevance.ACT-05: This is the Florida authority that a protective injunction under section 39.504 does not depend on an open dependency case.

cases.case_name: E.M.J. v. Department of Children & Families
cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, First District
cases.holding: Entering an injunction to prevent child abuse without holding a full evidentiary hearing once the respondent objected violated due process, and the injunction was reversed for an evidentiary hearing.
cases.quote: the trial court violated appellant's due process rights by not requiring the Department to prove its entitlement to an injunction under section 39.504 at a full evidentiary hearing

relevance.ACT-05: E.M.J. supplies the procedural floor for section 39.504 injunctions: the Department must prove entitlement at a contested evidentiary hearing.

cases.case_name: Department of Children & Family Services v. G.M.
cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, Fifth District
cases.holding: Surgery is not 'ordinary medical care' that the Department may authorize as legal custodian; certiorari was granted and the trial court directed to enter an order authorizing the procedure for the dependent child.
cases.quote: it is logical to conclude that surgery is excluded from the definition of "ordinary medical care" and "medical treatment."

relevance.INP-07: It marks the line between routine medical care the agency may consent to and treatment that requires judicial authorization.
relevance.ACT-06: G.M. is the Florida authority on who may authorize non-ordinary medical procedures for a child in state custody.

cases.case_name: E.G. v. Department of Children & Families
cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, Third District
cases.holding: Certiorari was granted quashing an order that directed a dependent minor to 'voluntarily' enter residential drug treatment and to abstain from running away, because the trial court lacked authority to compel that placement.
cases.quote: we agree with the Minor that the trial court lacked the authority to direct him to "voluntarily submit himself" to the residential treatment facility

relevance.INP-07: A crisis-stabilization admission and suitability assessments did not empower the court to order the residential placement the statute did not authorize.
relevance.ACT-06: E.G. limits court-ordered psychological and substance-abuse placements for dependent children to the procedures section 39.407 actually provides.
relevance.OUT-04: The order also purported to restrain an older foster youth from running away, and the court held that exceeded its authority.

cases.case_name: S.M. v. R.M.
cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, Fourth District
cases.holding: Treating the mother's appeal of a family court judge's sua sponte dependency shelter order as a certiorari petition, the court granted relief and remanded because she was given no opportunity to be heard or present evidence at the shelter hearing.
cases.quote: We treat the mother's appeal as a petition for writ of certiorari, grant the petition, and remand with directions.

relevance.INP-04: The shelter order here was entered by a judge on his own motion during a family-law proceeding, the court-initiated route into dependency.
relevance.INP-12: It defines the due-process minimum when a child is placed in shelter care: notice and a real opportunity to be heard.
relevance.DEC-04: A shelter order entered without hearing the parent departs from the essential requirements of law and is subject to certiorari.
relevance.DEC-05: The case shows what a court must do before shelter findings under section 39.402 can stand as the opening of a dependency case.
relevance.ACT-05: The same hearing requirements constrain orders restricting a parent's contact with the child entered at the shelter stage.

cases.case_name: In re S.A.R.D.
cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, Third District
cases.holding: Dismissal of a private dependency petition filed two days before the youth turned eighteen was affirmed because the record supported the finding that he had not been abandoned, abused or neglected by his mother.
cases.quote: we agree that S.A.R.D. failed to establish that he is a dependent child under Chapter 39, Florida Statutes (2015)

relevance.INP-05: S.A.R.D. shows the proof a youth must make when he petitions for dependency on his own behalf.
relevance.OUT-04: A petition filed on the eve of the youth's eighteenth birthday cannot substitute for statutory dependency grounds.
relevance.OUT-05: Where the statutory grounds are not proved, the correct outcome is dismissal rather than adjudication.

cases.case_name: Floyd v. Department of Children & Families
cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, First District
cases.holding: Summary judgment for the Department was reversed in a wrongful death action alleging that its investigator returned a child to a home with a known abuser, because reporting-related statutory immunity does not protect officials who fail to carry out their duty to protect the child.
cases.quote: it was not intended to protect those who fail to fulfill their duty to protect children

relevance.INP-01: Floyd separates immunity for making or acting on a report from liability for failing to act on what the reports disclosed.
relevance.DEC-01: Closing an investigation and returning the child despite reported indicators of abuse can be actionable negligence.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the leading Florida appellate decision on agency liability after a child's death following a child-protective investigation.
relevance.FAIL-04: Floyd applies Yamuni's case-by-case immunity analysis to a fatality that followed an investigator's decision to return the child.
relevance.FAIL-06: The opinion shows how the facts of an agency's handling of a fatal case are tested publicly in court rather than internally.
relevance.PMC-04: Fatality review findings translate into liability only through the duty analysis Floyd applies.
relevance.PMC-05: The litigation record is a principal route by which the agency's handling of a child death becomes public.

cases.case_name: T.L. v. Department of Children & Families
cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, Fourth District
cases.holding: The order denying the mother's motion for reunification and placing the children in permanent guardianship was reversed and the guardianship vacated because the finding that she had not substantially complied with her case plan lacked competent substantial evidence.
cases.quote: We vacate the order of permanent guardianship and reverse and remand for a new hearing on the Mother's motion for reunification.

relevance.ACT-02: A finding of non-compliance with a court-ordered case plan must rest on competent substantial evidence, not impression.
relevance.OUT-01: T.L. protects a parent's statutory motion for reunification from being defeated by unsupported compliance findings.
relevance.OUT-03: Permanent guardianship cannot be imposed as a substitute for a properly decided reunification motion.
relevance.FAIL-01: This is the Florida remedy when a permanency order rests on evidence that does not support it.

cases.case_name: In re J.B. (J.B. v. Department of Children & Family Services)
cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, Second District
cases.holding: An order placing children in permanent guardianship and terminating protective supervision was reversed because the procedure used did not produce an adequate evidentiary hearing on the facts required to support permanent guardianship.
cases.quote: the procedure used did not result in an adequate evidentiary hearing to establish the factual issues necessary to support an order of permanent guardianship

relevance.ACT-04: Placing children permanently with a kin or non-parent guardian requires findings made at a real evidentiary hearing.
relevance.OUT-03: J.B. states the evidentiary prerequisites for a permanent guardianship judgment in Florida.
relevance.FAIL-01: Ending supervision through a summary permanency procedure is reversible error.

cases.case_name: Department of Children & Families v. C.W.
cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, First District
cases.holding: On remand the trial court properly reweighed the section 39.810 manifest-best-interests factors, and its decision to deny termination and change the permanency goal to placement with a fit and willing relative was affirmed as supported by competent substantial evidence.
cases.quote: Finding that the trial court's order is based on competent substantial evidence, we affirm.

relevance.ACT-04: C.W. shows that a child's bond with a relative caregiver may properly drive the permanency goal, provided the statutory factors are weighed.
relevance.OUT-03: Placement with a fit and willing relative is a permissible permanency outcome when termination is not in the child's manifest best interests.

cases.case_name: E.R. v. Department of Children & Family Services
cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, Third District
cases.holding: Termination of the father's parental rights was reversed because the trial court's order was not supported by competent substantial evidence, where the Department's own counselor testified he was not a danger to his children.
cases.quote: We reverse because the trial court's order is not supported by competent, substantial evidence.

relevance.OUT-01: Where the agency's own evidence undercuts risk findings, the parent is entitled to continue toward reunification.
relevance.FAIL-01: E.R. is a Florida example of appellate reversal of a termination judgment for evidentiary insufficiency.

cases.case_name: Doe v. Kearney
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
cases.holding: Florida's emergency removal statute comports with due process, and the caseworker was entitled to judgment because the circumstances showed an objectively imminent danger to the children justifying removal without prior court authorization.
cases.quote: there was an objectively imminent danger to the Doe children so as to justify O'Brien's temporary removal of the children without prior court authorization

relevance.INP-03: Law-enforcement information about prior abuse allegations fed directly into the emergency removal decision reviewed here.
relevance.INP-10: The case traces the escalation from report to investigation to warrantless removal under section 39.401.
relevance.INP-12: Kearney is the controlling federal authority in Florida on protective custody taken without prior judicial approval.
relevance.DEC-02: It describes the investigative posture in which a Florida child protective investigator may act on probable cause.
relevance.DEC-04: Emergency removal without a court order is constitutional only where objectively imminent danger exists.
relevance.ACT-03: The constitutional test in Kearney governs the removal that precedes any foster placement.
relevance.FAIL-02: A removal unsupported by objectively imminent danger is precisely the unlawful removal this node describes, actionable under section 1983.

cases.case_name: Maddox v. Stephens
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
cases.holding: The caseworker was entitled to qualified immunity on the mother's substantive due process claim arising from the emergency custody of her medically fragile child with a grandmother, because no clearly established law made that conduct unconstitutional.
cases.quote: Because we hold that there has been no violation of clearly established substantive due process law, we need not decide whether Stephens' behavior actually violated Maddox's substantive due process rights.

relevance.INP-12: Maddox shows how emergency custody decisions grounded in a child's medical needs are reviewed in the Eleventh Circuit.
relevance.DEC-04: It illustrates the qualified-immunity barrier facing parents who challenge an emergency custody decision after the fact.
relevance.ACT-04: The child was placed with a grandmother under emergency custody, the kinship posture at issue here.
relevance.FAIL-02: The clearly-established-law requirement is the principal obstacle to damages for an allegedly wrongful removal in this circuit.

cases.case_name: Loftus v. Clark-Moore
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
cases.holding: Social workers who interviewed a child at school without her father's consent and threatened removal during an investigation the father had invited did not violate clearly established rights, and dismissal of his section 1983 complaint was affirmed.
cases.quote: Because neither social worker violated any clearly established federal civil rights in the investigation that Loftus had invited, we affirm the dismissal of Loftus's complaint against them.

relevance.INP-02: The investigation began with the father's own petition, the voluntary-report posture.
relevance.INP-05: A parent who asks the system for help cannot readily limit the investigation that follows.
relevance.INP-08: Loftus is the Eleventh Circuit authority on interviewing a child at school without parental notice or consent.
relevance.INP-10: It shows how a request for help escalates into a full child protective investigation of the requesting parent.
relevance.DEC-02: The case defines the interview and consent rules a Florida investigator must observe once a report is accepted.
relevance.DEC-06: An investigation conducted without a petition still carries coercive weight, including threats of removal.
relevance.ACT-01: Services offered through a contracted community-based provider were the vehicle for the intervention reviewed here.
relevance.FAIL-02: Threats to remove children, without an actual removal, did not violate clearly established law in this circuit.

cases.case_name: 31 Foster Children v. Bush
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
cases.holding: In a systemic challenge to Florida's foster care system, standing must be shown claim by claim; some plaintiffs' claims were moot and others were dismissed for lack of standing, leaving only counts for which a particular plaintiff demonstrated injury in fact.
cases.quote: Only Reggie B. has standing to pursue the procedural due process claims set out in Count II, because he is the only plaintiff who has demonstrated injury in fact

relevance.INP-09: This is the Eleventh Circuit template for systemic litigation aimed at Florida's child welfare agency as a whole.
relevance.ACT-03: The claims concerned conditions, safety and case planning for children already in Florida foster placements.
relevance.FAIL-03: It shows the justiciability limits on suits seeking to enforce federal child welfare standards against Florida officials.
relevance.FAIL-05: The complaint included a black-children subclass alleging racial discrimination in care, which the standing analysis governs.
relevance.PMC-01: Federal performance standards are enforced in court only through plaintiffs with concrete individual injury.
relevance.PMC-02: Systemic funding and administration failures are not litigable in the abstract under this standing analysis.
relevance.PMC-03: Bush marks the boundary between citizen oversight mechanisms and judicially cognizable claims.
relevance.PMC-06: Any accountability project relying on litigation must satisfy the claim-specific injury requirement stated here.

cases.case_name: Santosky v. Kramer
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Before a State may sever completely and irrevocably the rights of parents in their natural child, due process requires proof by at least clear and convincing evidence; New York's fair-preponderance standard was unconstitutional.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.DEC-03: Santosky is the federal floor that separates an administrative finding from the proof needed to sever parental rights.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the constitutional source of Florida's clear-and-convincing standard for termination of parental rights.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Federal Constitution does not require appointed counsel in every parental termination proceeding; whether due process requires counsel is decided case by case by the trial court, subject to appellate review.
cases.quote: leave the decision whether due process calls for the appointment of counsel for indigent parents in termination proceedings to be answered in the first instance by the trial court

relevance.DEC-05: Lassiter sets the federal floor for counsel once a petition that may end parental rights is filed; Florida's In re D.B. goes further.
relevance.FAIL-01: Whether the absence of counsel was reversible error is reviewed case by case on appeal under this standard.

cases.case_name: Troxel v. Granville
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Due Process Clause protects a fit parent's fundamental right to direct the care, custody and control of her children, and Washington's broad visitation statute as applied unconstitutionally infringed that right.
cases.quote: the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment protects the fundamental right of parents to make decisions concerning the care, custody, and control of their children

relevance.INP-12: Any protective custody decision interferes with the constitutionally protected parental interest Troxel describes.
relevance.DEC-04: Emergency removal is measured against the presumption that a fit parent acts in the child's best interests.
relevance.FAIL-02: Troxel supplies the substantive liberty interest that an unlawful removal invades.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative federal constitutional duty on a state agency to protect a child from violence by a private actor, so the agency's failure to remove Joshua DeShaney was not a constitutional violation.
cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

relevance.DEC-01: A decision to screen out or close a case is not itself a federal constitutional violation, which is why Florida tort law (Yamuni, Floyd) carries this node.
relevance.OUT-06: DeShaney is the reason fatality claims in Florida proceed under state negligence law rather than section 1983.
relevance.FAIL-02: It marks the boundary between failure to protect, which is not actionable federally, and affirmative removal, which is.
relevance.FAIL-03: Federal constitutional law supplies no general remedy for systemic protective failures.
relevance.FAIL-04: A child's death after agency involvement does not by itself establish a federal due process claim.
relevance.PMC-01: Federal monitoring, not constitutional litigation, is the mechanism for addressing systemic protective failures after DeShaney.

cases.case_name: Palmore v. Sidoti
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Reversing a Florida custody decision, the Court held that the possible effects of private racial prejudice cannot justify removing a child from the custody of a parent; such a racial classification cannot survive equal protection review.
cases.quote: Private biases may be outside the reach of the law, but the law cannot, directly or indirectly, give them effect.

relevance.FAIL-05: Palmore, itself a Florida case, is the controlling authority that race may not drive custody or placement decisions.

cases.case_name: Wyman v. James
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: A caseworker's periodic home visit required as a condition of AFDC benefits is a reasonable administrative tool that is not an unwarranted invasion of privacy and violates no Fourth Amendment right.
cases.quote: that it is not an unwarranted invasion of personal privacy; and that it violates no right guaranteed by the Fourth Amendment

relevance.INP-12: Wyman is the starting point for analyzing whether a caseworker's entry into a home is a Fourth Amendment search.
relevance.DEC-02: Home visits during a child protective assessment are evaluated against Wyman's administrative-visit framework rather than criminal search doctrine.

cases.case_name: Suter v. Artist M.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The 'reasonable efforts' requirement of the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act creates no privately enforceable right, so beneficiaries could not sue state child welfare officials under section 1983 to enforce it.
cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

relevance.INP-09: Because private enforcement is unavailable, federal reviews and audits are the practical oversight mechanism for Title IV-E compliance.
relevance.FAIL-03: Suter is why a state's failure to meet federal reasonable-efforts standards is remedied through funding processes, not private suits.
relevance.PMC-01: CFSR monitoring exists in the space Suter left open after foreclosing private enforcement of the Act.
relevance.PMC-02: Financial and audit remedies, not litigation, are the sanction for federal child welfare noncompliance.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen review panels and similar bodies operate as substitutes for judicially enforceable rights under the Act.
relevance.PMC-06: Any accountability analysis of Florida's federal compliance must account for the absence of a private right of action.

cases.case_name: Florida Department of Children & Families v. F.L.
cases.court: Supreme Court of Florida
cases.holding: Section 39.806(1)(i), which lets the Department petition for termination on the basis of a prior involuntary termination as to a sibling without first offering a case plan for the current child, is constitutional only if construed to require the State to prove — with no rebuttable presumption shifting the burden to the parent — a prior involuntary termination, a substantial risk of significant harm to the current child, and that termination is the least restrictive means of protecting that child.
cases.quote: Further, the state must prove that the termination of parental rights is the least restrictive means of protecting the current child from harm.

relevance.DEC-06: F.L. is the case that qualifies Padgett at the front end: the Department may proceed straight to a termination petition under section 39.806(1)(i) without first routing the family through a case plan, so long as it still carries the constitutional burden.
relevance.ACT-01: It establishes that no voluntary service plan need precede a petition grounded on a prior involuntary termination, which limits any argument that an offered voluntary plan is a universal prerequisite.
relevance.ACT-02: F.L. confirms that a court-ordered case plan is not a constitutional precondition to severance in every case, while insisting the State still prove substantial risk and least restrictive means.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification efforts are not required where the statutory ground is a prior involuntary termination, but the State must still prove the current child faces substantial risk of significant harm before reunification is ruled out.

cases.case_name: Trianon Park Condominium Ass'n v. City of Hialeah
cases.court: Supreme Court of Florida
cases.holding: Section 768.28 waived sovereign immunity but created no new causes of action; sorting governmental activity into four categories, the Court held there has never been a common-law duty to individual citizens for the enforcement of police-power functions, so the city was not liable for negligent building-code inspection.
cases.quote: First, for there to be governmental tort liability, there must be either an underlying common law or statutory duty of care with respect to the alleged negligent conduct.

relevance.DEC-01: Before a screen-out or closure can be actionable, Trianon Park requires the plaintiff to identify an underlying common-law or statutory duty of care, which is precisely the work Yamuni's statutory-duty holding does.
relevance.FAIL-04: This is the framework inside which every Florida claim against the child welfare agency is analyzed: category IV service functions can generate liability, category II enforcement functions cannot.
relevance.OUT-06: A wrongful-death claim after a child fatality survives only if the agency's conduct falls in a category where a duty of care exists, which is the threshold question Trianon Park poses.

cases.case_name: Wallace v. Dean
cases.court: Supreme Court of Florida
cases.holding: Where sheriff's deputies responded to a 911 call, engaged an unresponsive woman, conducted a safety check and assured others that no ambulance was needed, the undertaker's doctrine imposed a common-law duty of care, and because that conduct was operational rather than discretionary, sovereign immunity did not bar the wrongful-death claim.
cases.quote: we further hold that the affirmative actions of the deputies involved in this case were operational in nature; therefore, sovereign immunity does not bar the plaintiff-petitioner's negligence-based wrongful-death claim

relevance.DEC-01: Wallace is the modern statement of when a government actor who undertakes to check on a person at risk assumes a duty, which is the analysis applied when an investigator looks in on a reported child and then closes the case.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the current Florida Supreme Court restatement of the duty and operational/discretionary analysis that a court will apply to a Yamuni-style claim, so FAIL-04 no longer rests on a 1988 decision alone.
relevance.OUT-06: Wallace supplies the undertaker's-doctrine route to a negligence-based wrongful-death claim against a government defendant after a death that followed an official safety check.

cases.case_name: Beagle v. Beagle
cases.court: Supreme Court of Florida
cases.holding: Section 752.01(1)(e) was facially unconstitutional under article I, section 23 of the Florida Constitution because it authorized court-ordered grandparent visitation in an intact family on a best-interests test without requiring any showing that the child is threatened with harm.
cases.quote: the State may not intrude upon the parents' fundamental right to raise their children except in cases where the child is threatened with harm

relevance.INP-12: Beagle gives Florida practitioners a binding state constitutional premise — the express right of privacy — for challenging protective custody, stronger than Troxel's four-Justice plurality.
relevance.DEC-04: Any emergency removal must be justified by demonstrable harm or threatened harm to the child, not by a court's view of the child's best interests.
relevance.FAIL-02: It supplies the state constitutional liberty and privacy interest that an unlawful removal invades, independent of federal substantive due process.

cases.case_name: Von Eiff v. Azicri
cases.court: Supreme Court of Florida
cases.holding: Section 752.01(1)(a), which required a court to award grandparent visitation on a best-interests finding when a parent has died, is facially unconstitutional under Florida's right of privacy because it permits state intrusion on a fit parent's decision without proof of demonstrable harm to the child or any compelling state interest.
cases.quote: government interference in a parent's decision to exclude or limit grandparental visitation cannot be countenanced without a showing of a compelling state interest

relevance.DEC-04: Von Eiff confirms that a bare best-interests judgment cannot support state intrusion into a fit parent's decisions, which is the standard against which an emergency removal decision must be measured in Florida.
relevance.DEC-06: Non-adjudicatory intervention in a family's life still engages the parents' constitutional privacy right, so differential-response contact with a fit family cannot rest on best-interests reasoning alone.

cases.case_name: Stanley v. Illinois
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Illinois could not presume unwed fathers unfit and make their children wards of the State without a hearing; due process entitled Stanley to a hearing on his parental fitness, and denying him the hearing afforded all other parents denied him equal protection.
cases.quote: as a matter of due process of law, Stanley was entitled to a hearing on his fitness as a parent before his children were taken from him

relevance.DEC-05: Stanley is the foundational federal holding that a petition which will take a parent's children cannot be resolved without an individualized hearing on that parent's fitness.
relevance.ACT-03: Children may not be placed with court-appointed guardians on a statutory presumption of unfitness; the placement must follow a fitness hearing.

cases.case_name: M. L. B. v. S. L. J.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: A State may not condition an indigent parent's appeal from a decree terminating parental rights on her ability to advance record preparation fees; Mississippi had to furnish a record sufficient to permit appellate review of the sufficiency of the evidence.
cases.quote: Mississippi may not deny M. L. B., because of her poverty, appellate review of the sufficiency of the evidence on which the trial court found her unfit to remain a parent

relevance.FAIL-01: M.L.B. guarantees that the appellate remedy for an erroneous termination judgment is actually available to an indigent parent, which is the precondition for the court-reversal route this node describes.

cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: 'Domicile' in ICWA section 1911(a) is defined by uniform federal law, not state law; twins born off-reservation to parents domiciled on the Choctaw reservation were themselves domiciled there, so the tribal court had exclusive jurisdiction and the state adoption decree was reversed.
cases.quote: These congressional objectives make clear that a rule of domicile that would permit individual Indian parents to defeat the ICWA's jurisdictional scheme is inconsistent with what Congress intended

relevance.INP-11: Holyfield is the Supreme Court's foundational ICWA decision and the starting point for any Florida jurisdictional analysis involving an Indian child, including the threshold question of exclusive tribal jurisdiction.
relevance.FAIL-05: It grounds ICWA in Congress's finding that Indian children were being removed from their families and culture by non-tribal agencies, which is the interest the placement-preference and deviation rules protect.

cases.case_name: Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: ICWA section 1912(f)'s beyond-a-reasonable-doubt 'continued custody' requirement does not apply to a parent who never had custody, section 1912(d)'s remedial-efforts requirement applies only where termination would precipitate the breakup of an Indian family, and section 1915(a)'s preferences do not bar a non-Indian adoption when no preferred party has sought to adopt.
cases.quote: §1912(f) does not apply where the Indian parent never had custody of the Indian child.

relevance.INP-11: Adoptive Couple directly qualifies the beyond-a-reasonable-doubt proposition Florida's J.P.H. draws from section 1912(f), so INP-11 overstates that holding without it.
relevance.ACT-04: It narrows section 1915(a), holding the placement preferences do not displace an adoption where no preferred relative or tribal family has actually come forward.

cases.case_name: Haaland v. Brackeen
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court upheld Congress's Article I authority to enact ICWA and rejected the anticommandeering challenges on the merits, while vacating the equal protection and nondelegation rulings because no petitioner had standing to press them.
cases.quote: the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners' challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing

relevance.INP-11: Brackeen is the current baseline for ICWA's constitutional validity and binding force on Florida state courts, and it is the authority a 2026-dated brief must cite alongside the older Florida DCA decisions.
relevance.ACT-04: It leaves ICWA's placement-preference scheme intact and in force, so section 1915 continues to govern kinship and tribal placement of Indian children in Florida.
relevance.FAIL-05: The equal protection challenge to ICWA's preferences was dismissed for want of standing rather than rejected on the merits, so the race-classification question remains open and must be described as unresolved.

notes: METHOD: Every case in this brief was retrieved from the CourtListener v4 API during this session (search + opinion text endpoints) and its opinion text read. Each quote was machine-verified as an exact substring of the retrieved opinion text (whitespace and curly-quote normalization only, no ellipses). Searches ran in order fla -> fladistctapp -> ca11/scotus.

EXISTING key_cases IN THE FL FILES: the titles in layers.case_law.key_cases across the 42 FL node files are keyword-matched noise (Justia listings of rule-amendment opinions such as 'In Re: Amendments to Florida Rules of Juvenile Procedure', with synthetic citations like 'Florida Supreme Court Case sc2023-1072 (2024)'). I looked them up; none was on point for any node and none was retained. Only 'Askew v. Florida DCF' looked promising by title and did not survive review.

NO UNPUBLISHED MEMORANDUM DECISIONS WERE USED. All entries are published state supreme court, published district court of appeal, published Eleventh Circuit, or U.S. Supreme Court opinions. The one exception on citation form is Statewide Guardian ad Litem Office v. C.C. (Fla. Mar. 7, 2024), a published Florida Supreme Court merits opinion for which CourtListener's cluster carries no reporter citation; it is given in slip form (No. SC2023-0604). Counsel should update to the So. 3d cite before filing. Haaland v. Brackeen's cluster likewise carries only the U.S. Reports cite (599 U.S. 255), which is sufficient.

TROXEL v. GRANVILLE: the quoted passage is from Justice O'Connor's controlling plurality opinion (four Justices); there was no majority opinion. It is cited here for the parental-liberty premise that Florida courts and the Eleventh Circuit apply, not as a holding of five Justices. With Beagle and Von Eiff now added, INP-12, DEC-04 and FAIL-02 no longer depend on Troxel alone: Florida's own constitutional privacy line is binding rather than persuasive.
LASSITER date_decided (1981-08-28) is CourtListener's date_filed for the cluster, which reflects the denial of rehearing; the opinion issued June 1, 1981. Year is given as 1981.

GAPS - CENTRAL ABUSE REGISTRY / VERIFIED-FINDING DUE PROCESS: I found no Florida Supreme Court or DCA decision on the record in this session squarely establishing a parent's right to an administrative hearing to challenge or expunge a verified abuse finding in the Florida central abuse hotline record. DEC-03 is therefore built on the adjudicatory-proof line (DHRS v. M.B., R.F. v. DCF, Padgett) plus Santosky's federal floor. A lawyer relying on DEC-03 for registry-challenge work should research Fla. Stat. ss. 39.301(20) and ch. 120 administrative remedies separately.

GAPS - EXTENDED FOSTER CARE (OUT-04): no published Florida appellate decision construing the extended foster care / PESS provisions (Fla. Stat. ss. 39.6251, 39.013(2)) surfaced in these searches. OUT-04 is carried by S.A.R.D. (dependency jurisdiction for a youth approaching 18) and E.G. (limits on court control over an older foster youth). This node remains at the two-case minimum and should be supplemented with statutory and DCF rule authority.

GAPS - MISSING / ABSCONDED CHILDREN FROM CARE: no Florida appellate authority located on agency duties when a child goes missing from foster care. E.G. v. DCF is the closest (a court order directing a dependent minor not to run away was quashed as beyond the court's authority).

GAPS - PMC FAMILY (PMC-01 through PMC-06): CFSR monitoring, OIG/Single Audit review, CAPTA citizen review panels, the Protect Our Kids Act commission and FOIA-style transparency are administrative and statutory constructs with essentially no direct case law. These nodes are mapped to the nearest enforceable-law authority: Suter v. Artist M. (no private right to enforce Title IV-E reasonable efforts), Foster Children v. Bush (claim-by-claim standing limits on systemic suits), DeShaney (no federal constitutional duty to protect), and the Florida public-records line (Sarasota Herald-Tribune, Gainesville Sun, Floyd). This is the federal/state standard, offered as such, not a claim that courts have ruled on CFSR or citizen review panels.

ICWA (INP-11): Florida has no state ICWA statute; the node rests on federal ICWA as applied by Florida DCAs and by the U.S. Supreme Court. J.P.H. (1st DCA 2010) remains the strongest Florida holding, but it must now be read with Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl and Haaland v. Brackeen, both added in this pass. No Florida decision retrieved addresses transfer to tribal court or the qualified-expert-witness requirement of s. 1912(e)-(f) in any depth.

SECTION 1983 REMOVAL LAW (FAIL-02, DEC-04, INP-12): Florida's federal circuit is the Eleventh, and the governing trio is Doe v. Kearney (warrantless emergency removal requires objectively imminent danger; Fla. Stat. s. 39.401(1) upheld), Maddox v. Stephens (qualified immunity where no clearly established law) and Loftus v. Clark-Moore (no clearly established right against school interview without parental consent, or against threats of removal). Practitioners should note how heavily the 'clearly established' requirement favors defendants in this circuit, and should plead the Florida constitutional privacy right (Beagle, Von Eiff) alongside the federal claim.

AGENCY TORT LIABILITY (FAIL-04, OUT-06, DEC-01): unlike the federal constitutional route foreclosed by DeShaney, Florida recognizes a state-law duty. The full chain is now in the brief: Trianon Park (1985) supplies the four-category threshold duty analysis, Yamuni (1988) holds the agency owes a statutory duty of care once abuse reports are received and that caseworker conduct is operational-level activity, Wallace v. Dean (2009) is the modern restatement of duty plus the operational/discretionary test and the undertaker's doctrine, and Floyd (1st DCA 2003) applies the line to a fatality. Damages remain capped by s. 768.28(5).

STATUTORY RENUMBERING: Padgett (1991), Yamuni (1988) and In re D.B. (1980) construe the pre-1998 statutes (ch. 39 as then numbered, ch. 415, ch. 827). Their constitutional holdings remain controlling and are routinely applied to current ch. 39, but the section numbers quoted in those opinions no longer correspond to current law.

QUOTE FORM: several quotes are complete clauses rather than complete sentences, taken mid-sentence to stay within the 30-word limit while keeping the rule and its qualifier intact - DHRS v. M.B., Lassiter, Beagle, M.L.B., Wallace v. Dean, Holyfield and Brackeen. Seminole Tribe's quote is from footnote 3 of the majority opinion, which is where the court states the standard of review it adopts. Every quote is from the majority (or, for Troxel, the controlling plurality), never a concurrence, dissent, syllabus or statement of facts.

NODE_MAP RECONCILIATION: the prior brief's node_map omitted eleven case-node pairs that the case entries' own relevance objects already declared. Those were added without any new research: M.B. at ACT-06; R.F. at INP-10; DCF v. J.D. at INP-03 and INP-04; G.M. and E.G. at INP-07; Floyd at FAIL-06 and PMC-05; Loftus at INP-02 and INP-08; Wyman at INP-12. This alone cured the two coverage deficits (INP-04 and INP-07 had been listed with one case each).

Added Florida Department of Children & Families v. F.L., 880 So. 2d 602 (Fla. 2004) for DEC-06, ACT-01, ACT-02, OUT-01: it is the qualification on Padgett that the brief lacked, holding that section 39.806(1)(i) lets the Department seek termination on the strength of a prior involuntary termination without first offering a case plan for the current child, while still requiring clear and convincing proof of substantial risk and least restrictive means with no burden shifted to the parent. CORRECTION TO THE VERIFIER'S GLOSS: F.L. does not hold in terms that 'the Department need not offer a case plan or reunification services in every case'; the majority upholds a statutory ground that operates without a case-plan prerequisite and expressly reaffirms that the least-restrictive-means and substantial-risk burdens stay on the State in every case. F.L. also bears directly on OUT-02, but OUT-02 already carries the maximum six authorities (Padgett, Santosky, S.M., J.B., C.C., In re D.B.), so it is mapped at the four nodes above; counsel briefing OUT-02 should cite F.L. alongside Padgett.

Added Trianon Park Condominium Ass'n v. City of Hialeah, 468 So. 2d 912 (Fla. 1985) for DEC-01, FAIL-04, OUT-06: it is the threshold framework a Florida court applies before reaching Yamuni, holding that section 768.28 created no new causes of action and that governmental tort liability requires an underlying common-law or statutory duty of care, with no such duty for category II police-power enforcement functions.

Added Wallace v. Dean, 3 So. 3d 1035 (Fla. 2009) for DEC-01, FAIL-04, OUT-06: it is the current Florida Supreme Court statement of the duty analysis, the operational/discretionary line and the undertaker's doctrine as applied to government actors who respond, engage a person at risk and then leave, so agency-liability nodes no longer rest on a 1988 decision alone.

Added Beagle v. Beagle, 678 So. 2d 1271 (Fla. 1996) for INP-12, DEC-04, FAIL-02: it supplies a binding Florida constitutional premise — article I, section 23 privacy — that the State may not intrude on parental decision-making except where the child is threatened with harm, which is stronger in a Florida court than Troxel's four-Justice plurality.

Added Von Eiff v. Azicri, 720 So. 2d 510 (Fla. 1998) for DEC-04, DEC-06: it extends Beagle to a widowed parent and holds that a bare best-interests standard cannot justify state interference absent a compelling interest and proof of demonstrable harm, which is the anchor for testing both emergency removal and non-adjudicatory intervention. Von Eiff also reinforces FAIL-02, but FAIL-02 reached the six-case maximum with Beagle.

Added Stanley v. Illinois, 405 U.S. 645 (1972) for DEC-05, ACT-03: it is the foundational federal holding that a parent is entitled to a hearing on fitness before the State takes the children, the natural companion to Santosky and Lassiter. It equally supports INP-12 and DEC-04, but both nodes reached the six-case maximum with Wyman/Beagle and Beagle/Von Eiff respectively.

Added M. L. B. v. S. L. J., 519 U.S. 102 (1996) for FAIL-01: a State may not condition appeal from a termination decree on the parent's ability to pay record preparation fees, which is the precondition for the appellate-reversal remedy this node describes. It also belongs at OUT-02, which is at the six-case maximum.

Added Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield, 490 U.S. 30 (1989) for INP-11, FAIL-05: the Supreme Court's foundational ICWA decision, holding that 'domicile' under section 1911(a) is a matter of uniform federal law and that parents cannot defeat exclusive tribal jurisdiction by arranging an off-reservation birth.

Added Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl, 570 U.S. 637 (2013) for INP-11, ACT-04: it narrows ICWA sections 1912(f), 1912(d) and 1915(a) and directly qualifies the beyond-a-reasonable-doubt proposition the brief draws from J.P.H., so citing J.P.H. without it overstates that holding.

Added Haaland v. Brackeen, 599 U.S. 255 (2023) for INP-11, ACT-04, FAIL-05: it is the current baseline for ICWA's validity, rejecting the Article I and anticommandeering challenges on the merits and disposing of the equal protection and nondelegation challenges for lack of standing — which means the race-classification question about section 1915's preferences is unresolved, not settled.

AUTHORITIES NOT VERIFIED: none. All ten authorities the verifier flagged as missing were located on CourtListener in this session, their clusters and opinions retrieved, and their opinion texts read; all ten are real, on point, and have been added. The only correction to the verifier's descriptions is to F.L., noted above.

INP-04 (court-ordered referral) FOLLOW-UP: after the node_map reconciliation this node carries two retrieved, on-point Florida decisions (S.M. v. R.M., where a family-court judge entered a sua sponte shelter order, and DCF v. J.D., on the circuit court's own jurisdiction over a protective-injunction petition with no dependency case open). Additional fla and fladistctapp searches for a Florida decision squarely construing a judge's power to order a child-protective investigation in a pending civil or criminal case returned nothing stronger, so this node stays at the two-case minimum by design rather than by omission.

Missing (for a later pass): Commercial Carrier Corp. v. Indian River County, 371 So. 2d 1010 (Fla. 1979) — the foundational Florida Supreme Court decision adopting the operational/planning (discretionary) distinction under s. 768.28. Trianon Park and Wallace v. Dean both build on it and Trianon cites it by name in the very passage the brief quotes; DEC-01, FAIL-04 and OUT-06 are incomplete without it.

Missing (for a later pass): Taylor v. Ledbetter, 818 F.2d 791 (11th Cir. 1987) (en banc) — holds that a child involuntarily placed in state foster care has a substantive due process liberty interest in safe conditions actionable under s. 1983. This is the Eleventh Circuit's answer to DeShaney's 'custody' exception and is the missing counterweight at ACT-03, FAIL-04 and OUT-06, where the brief currently presents federal liability as wholly foreclosed.

Missing (for a later pass): Rayburn ex rel. Rayburn v. Hogue, 241 F.3d 1341 (11th Cir. 2001) — addresses the limits of the special-relationship/state-action theory for harm inflicted by foster parents, bounding Taylor v. Ledbetter. A practitioner briefing FAIL-04 or OUT-06 in Florida would be expected to cite it alongside Taylor.

Missing (for a later pass): State v. Townsend, 635 So. 2d 949 (Fla. 1994) — the Florida Supreme Court's statement of the reliability findings required under s. 90.803(23) for a child victim's out-of-court statements. DHRS v. M.B. applies this framework; INP-08 and DEC-03 cite M.B. without the case that supplies the reliability test itself.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Adoption of Baby E.A.W., 658 So. 2d 961 (Fla. 1995) — the Florida Supreme Court's leading treatment of abandonment as a ground for severance and of the weight given a parent's conduct toward the child. OUT-02 currently carries the standard of proof and the permanency hierarchy but no authority on the substantive statutory grounds.
